**The Minute With Sixty-One Seconds**

On the last day of 2016, at the very end of the day as reckoned in Greenwich, the clocks that govern the world did something that clocks are not supposed to do. They ticked from 23:59:59 to 23:59:60. Then, a second later, they arrived at 00:00:00 and the new year began, one second later than it would have otherwise. Almost nobody noticed. Those who did notice mostly noticed because something broke.

I want to write about that extra second, because I think it is one of the strangest and most quietly moving artifacts of modern civilization, and because it is about to disappear.

---

The leap second exists because there are two different answers to the question *what is a second?*, and the two answers do not agree.

The older answer is that a second is a fraction of a day: one eighty-six-thousand-four-hundredth of the time it takes the Earth to turn once beneath the sun. This is the second that grows out of ordinary experience. Noon is when the sun is highest; a day is the interval between noons; hours, minutes, and seconds are just the day sliced finer and finer. For most of human history, this was the only definition anyone needed. The sky was the clock, and everything else—sundials, water clocks, pendulums, springs—was an attempt to imitate it.

The newer answer, adopted in 1967, is that a second is the duration of 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation emitted when a cesium-133 atom flips between two particular energy states. This number was chosen so that the new second would match the old one as closely as anyone could measure at the time. But it was a snapshot. It froze the length of the second at what the Earth's rotation happened to be during a particular stretch of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

The problem is that the Earth is not a good clock.

It is a spectacularly good clock by the standards of anything humans built before the twentieth century. But held against a cesium atom, it wobbles. The moon drags the oceans, and the oceans drag on the seabed, and the friction bleeds away a little rotational energy every day, so that on average the planet turns slightly slower each century than the last. But only on average. The molten outer core sloshes against the mantle and exchanges angular momentum with it. Ice sheets melt and the water redistributes toward the equator, changing the planet's shape and, with it, its spin, the way a skater slows when she extends her arms. Great earthquakes shift enough mass to shave microseconds off the day. Weather matters. The winds of El Niño years measurably alter the length of a day. And in the early 2020s, for reasons not fully understood, the Earth began spinning slightly *faster* than it had in decades, which had never been observed since precise measurement began and which threatened, for the first time, to require a *negative* leap second—a minute with fifty-nine seconds—something no one had ever attempted and no software had ever been tested against.

So the two seconds drift apart. The atomic second is fixed and perfect and indifferent. The astronomical second stretches and shrinks with the temperament of the planet. Left alone, atomic time would slowly pull ahead of solar time, and eventually—not soon, but eventually—the clocks would say noon while the sun was still climbing.

The leap second was the patch. Since 1972, whenever the difference between atomic time and astronomical time approached nine-tenths of a second, the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (an organization that really exists, and whose name I find wonderful) announced that an extra second would be inserted at the end of June or December. Twenty-seven times this happened. Every one of them was a positive second, an addition, a minute of sixty-one. The Earth was, over the long run, slowing down, and time itself was being padded to keep pace with it.

---

There is something I find almost unbearably touching in this arrangement, and I want to try to say what it is.

The leap second is an act of fidelity. Humanity had built, in the cesium clock, a timekeeper vastly better than the sky—more regular, more portable, more universal. Every cesium atom in the universe is identical; the frequency of that hyperfine transition is the same in Paris and in Tokyo and, presumably, in the Andromeda galaxy. The Earth's rotation, by contrast, is provincial. It belongs to one planet. It is contingent on the accidents of the moon's distance and the arrangement of continents and the amount of ice sitting on Greenland. From the standpoint of physics, there is no reason to prefer it.

And yet, for fifty years, we chose it. We took the perfect clock and periodically stopped it for a beat so that it would not leave the imperfect sky behind. We insisted that noon should still mean *the sun is overhead*, that the number on the clock should still refer, however loosely, to where we are in relation to our star. The leap second was a little cord tying the abstract to the actual, the atom to the afternoon.

It was also, in practice, a headache.

Computers do not like minutes with sixty-one seconds. Most software assumes, quite reasonably, that after 59 comes 00. When the leap second arrived at the end of June 2012, a bug in the Linux kernel's handling of it caused servers across the world to lock up. Reddit went down. So did parts of Mozilla, LinkedIn, Yelp. Airline reservation systems in Australia failed, stranding passengers at check-in counters while the extra second worked its way through their infrastructure. Google, having been burned earlier, had already invented the "leap smear": rather than inserting a whole second at once, its servers would stretch every second across a window of hours by a tiny imperceptible amount, so that the extra time got absorbed without any clock ever displaying a number that shouldn't exist. Other companies adopted their own smears, of differing lengths and shapes, which meant that during the smear windows, different parts of the internet quietly disagreed about what time it was.

The financial markets, where trades are timestamped to the microsecond and where being a millisecond out of sync with your counterparty can constitute a legal dispute, hated the leap second. Satellite navigation systems handled it, but each one differently: GPS time does not include leap seconds at all and is now eighteen seconds ahead of civil time, a discrepancy carried in a correction field that receivers must remember to apply. Every leap second was a small global coordination problem with no upside except the preservation of a relationship between clocks and the sky that almost no one, in their daily lives, could perceive.

So in November 2022, at the General Conference on Weights and Measures in Versailles—the body that decides what a kilogram is, what a meter is, what a second is—the delegates voted to let the sky go. Leap seconds would continue until 2035 at the latest, and then stop. After that, atomic time and solar time would be permitted to drift apart, and some future generation, perhaps a century from now, would decide what, if anything, to do about it.

---

It is worth being clear about the scale of the drift, because it is easy to imagine either too much or too little.

The accumulated gap between atomic and solar time, over the fifty years the leap second was in force, was twenty-seven seconds. If the Earth keeps decelerating at roughly its long-term rate—and it may not, since the recent speeding-up shows how little we can predict it—the gap would grow to about a minute within a century of leap seconds ending. An hour would take something like several thousand years. There is no scenario in which anyone alive today, or anyone whose grandchildren are alive today, will look at a clock reading noon and see the sun anywhere but roughly overhead.

So in one sense the decision changes nothing. In another sense it changes something I want to name carefully.

For the first time, official time will be defined with no reference to the sky at all. Not adjusted to the sky, not corrected against the sky, not tied to the sky by a cord that occasionally gets tugged. Time will be what the atoms say it is, full stop, and the sun will do whatever the sun does.

---

I keep wanting to say that this is a loss, and I keep catching myself, because the story of timekeeping is a story of exactly this kind of loss, repeated, and we have survived every prior instance without noticing we'd lost anything.

Before 1883, every town in America kept its own time. Noon was when the sun was highest *there*, and a town fifty miles east reached noon a few minutes earlier. This was perfectly sensible until railroads made it necessary for people in different towns to agree on when a train would arrive, at which point it became chaos. The railroads imposed standard time zones—broad bands within which everyone would pretend the sun was overhead at the same moment—and within a generation nobody remembered that clock noon and sun noon had ever been the same thing. Today, in the western edge of a time zone, the sun may not be highest until nearly one o'clock, and no one experiences this as a discrepancy. The clock is the clock.

Daylight saving time pushes the disconnect further, and deliberately: we set our clocks an hour off from the sun for half the year because we have decided that the number on the clock, not the position of the sun, is what governs when we get up and go to work, and we would rather move the number than move ourselves.

And in 1582, Pope Gregory XIII deleted ten days. The Julian calendar had been drifting against the seasons for centuries, gaining about three days every four hundred years, until the spring equinox, which was supposed to fall around March 21, had slipped to March 11. The fix was simply to skip from October 4 to October 15. People went to bed on the fourth and woke on the fifteenth. There were riots in some places, and Protestant countries refused the papal calendar for a century or more, so that a traveler crossing from Catholic to Protestant lands would move ten days backward in time. But the equinox was restored to its proper date, and the calendar was once again tied to the sky, and the rioters' grandchildren could not have told you what the fuss was about.

In each case the pattern is the same. A human system of time is invented that matches the sky. The sky, or human needs, or both, drift. There is a crisis of coordination. A correction is applied—sometimes toward the sky, sometimes away from it—and the correction is briefly felt as an outrage against the natural order and then forgotten completely.

The leap second's abolition is one more turn of this wheel. The only difference is the direction. Most prior reforms were efforts to *recapture* the sky—to drag the calendar back to the equinox, to keep noon roughly meaning noon. This one is an agreement to stop trying.

---

I said I wanted to name the loss carefully, so let me try.

It is not that anything practical will change. It is not even, really, that the sky is being abandoned; the sky was never ours, and its indifference to our clocks is total. What is being given up is a *gesture*—a ritual, twenty-seven times performed, of pausing the perfect machine so that the imperfect world could catch up.

There was a humility in it. The cesium clock is one of the great triumphs of human ingenuity; it can hold time to within a second over hundreds of millions of years. And for half a century we treated that triumph as subordinate to the wobbling of a rock. We said, in effect: our instrument is better than the planet, but the planet is where we live, and we will bend the instrument to the planet rather than the other way around.

Now we will bend the other way. The reasons are good. Software is brittle; coordination is hard; nobody can feel a second. And in truth, the atom is not less natural than the sun. A cesium atom is as much a part of the world as a sunrise, and arguably a more honest one: it does not pretend to regularity it lacks. To take the atom as the standard is, in one light, a deeper respect for nature—for the nature that is everywhere the same, rather than the nature that happens to be nearby.

But I notice that the nature that happens to be nearby is the only kind any of us has ever lived in. The hyperfine transition of cesium-133 is a fact about the universe. The length of the day is a fact about *here*. And there is something in the decision to define time by the former that feels like a small further step out of *here*—toward a frame of reference in which location doesn't matter, in which the number is the same on every screen on every continent and refers to nothing outside the network of screens.

This is, I recognize, the same complaint the villagers made about railroad time, and I recognize also that I would not want to live in a world where every town kept its own noon. I am not arguing for the leap second's return. I am only trying to look at it clearly before it goes, the way one looks at a building scheduled for demolition, not because it should be saved but because it will soon be impossible to see.

---

The last leap second was inserted at the end of 2016. There has not been one since, because the Earth, in its unpredictable way, stopped slowing down and started speeding up, and the gap has held steady or shrunk. It is possible that there will never be another. It is possible that the leap second of December 31, 2016—the one that took down a few websites and delayed the new year by a beat—was the final performance of a ritual that lasted forty-four years and that nobody knew, at the time, to mark as an ending.

I like to imagine that moment. Somewhere in a data center, a clock displays 23:59:60—a time that, by the ordinary logic of minutes, cannot exist. Around the world, a few thousand engineers are awake and watching their dashboards, waiting to see what breaks. Everyone else is at a party, or asleep, or watching fireworks that are, unknown to them, going off one second late. And the planet, which has been turning a little too slowly for a while now, gets one second of grace: one second in which the machines wait for it.

Then the second is over. The clocks resume. The year begins.

I don't know what to call the feeling this gives me. It is not exactly nostalgia, since I never experienced leap seconds as anything but data. It is something more like the feeling of learning that a word you'd always assumed was permanent has quietly fallen out of a dictionary. The world goes on being describable without it. But the shape of what could be said has changed by one small notch, and there is a version of noon that will never again be quite what it was.
